stories.title: The Weaver and the Wind
stories.setting: East African and familiar learner contexts

parts.passageScript:
In a small village near the coast, there lived a woman named Dina who was known across the whole region for her extraordinary skill at weaving. Her cloths were so beautiful that merchants travelled from distant towns just to buy them. The patterns she created were unlike anything anyone had ever seen, with swirling designs of deep blue and gold that seemed to shimmer in the sunlight. People often said that Dina's fingers moved as if they were guided by the wind itself.
Dina was proud of her talent, and she guarded her methods very closely. Whenever younger women in the village asked her to teach them her techniques, she always refused. "These skills took me many years to master," she would say, shaking her head firmly. "Why should I simply give them away? My knowledge is the very thing that makes my cloth so valuable."
Her neighbour was an elderly man named Zane, who often watched her work from his doorstep. He had lived in the village his whole life, and everyone respected him for his patience and wisdom. "Dina," he said gently one morning, stepping a little closer to her loom, "a river that refuses to share its water slowly becomes a swamp. It grows stale, and in the end it turns useless."
"I am no river, Uncle," Dina replied, with a polite but dismissive smile. "I am more like a deep well, and my water is meant for my own family alone. I have worked hard to fill it, and I will not let strangers take from it." Zane shook his head sadly, but he said nothing more, for he had learned long ago that people must discover certain truths for themselves.
One evening, dark clouds gathered along the horizon. The monsoon winds arrived far earlier than anyone had expected, howling through the village with tremendous force. Dina rushed outside to protect her precious loom, but the wind was simply too powerful for her. It tore through her workshop like a wild animal, snapping the wooden frame and scattering her finest silk threads across the muddy ground. The heavy rain that followed soaked everything it touched. By morning, her workshop lay in ruins, and her loom, her thread, and her finished cloths had all been destroyed.
Dina sat among the wreckage with tears streaming down her face. She had no money to replace her loom, and the silk merchants would not return for many long months. Without her weaving, she had no way to earn a living for her family. For the very first time in her whole life, she felt completely helpless.

To Dina's great surprise, the village women arrived at her door the very next morning. "We cannot weave as finely as you can, Dina," said Sana, a young mother who carried her baby on her hip. "But we can certainly help you rebuild your loom. My husband is a carpenter, and he has already started cutting the wood."
"And I can spin fresh thread for you," added Alina, an older woman with strong, hardworking hands. "It will not be smooth silk, but it will be strong and good." One by one, the villagers offered whatever they could. A farmer brought sturdy planks of wood, and a fisherman donated thick rope for the frame. Even the children joined in, gathering the scattered threads from the bushes and fences where the wind had carried them. By the end of the day, Dina's yard was full of people working side by side.
Within a single week, Dina had a brand-new loom. It was different from the old one, rougher in some places and improvised in others, yet it was sturdy and very well built. The thread that Alina had spun was coarser than silk, but when Dina wove with it, something remarkable happened. The cloth she produced had a completely new quality, for it was thicker, warmer, and far more durable than anything she had made before. It was not delicate silk, but it was truly beautiful in its own honest way.
Dina stood before the finished cloth and felt something shift quietly inside her. She turned to the villagers who had helped her and said, "I have been foolish. For years I kept my skill locked away, believing it was mine alone to protect. But look at what we have made together, something far stronger and more useful than anything I ever created on my own."
She paused, looking at the faces around her. "From this day on, I will teach anyone who truly wishes to learn. My knowledge is not made smaller by sharing it. Instead, it is multiplied." Zane, watching from his doorstep as he always did, smiled broadly. "Now the river flows again," he said, "and the whole village will grow green because of it."
In the months that followed, Dina taught twelve women to weave, and each one slowly developed her own patterns and style. The village became famous not for one weaver, but for many, and their cloths were sold in busy markets right along the coast.
The moral of this fable is simple. A single thread breaks easily, but many threads woven together can weather any storm. Sharing what you know does not make you weaker; it makes your whole community stronger.

stories.title: Voices in the Chamber
stories.setting: East African and familiar learner contexts

parts.passageScript:
Long before independence, on the coast, the busy port town of Kalimani was ruled by distant foreign powers. A tall flag flew over the old chamber, where the laws were written, but those laws were never made for the local people. Twelve-year-old Kian lived in Kalimani with his younger sister, Zara. Their father worked as a boat builder, and their mother ran a small tea stall down by the shore. Although the family was poor, they always spoke with quiet pride.
"Freedom is not just for kings and rulers," their father often said. "Even a fisherman deserves to be heard." One day, a notice suddenly appeared on the market wall, announcing that officials from the northern parliament would hold a public discussion about new trade laws. "Another law?" Zara frowned. "Without ever asking us again?"
Kian had never once been inside the council chamber, but he had heard many whispers. People said illegal taxes were coming. Others quietly feared a blockade of the coast if the villagers dared to resist. At home that evening, Father sighed heavily. "We've been supplied with little, and asked to give much," he said. Mother nodded and added, "These new laws, none of them reflect our voice."
Kian could not sleep at all that night. He had recently read about emancipation in a borrowed history book, and the ideas would not leave him alone. "I have learned," he whispered into the dark, "that real change always comes from voices, from people who finally refuse to stay silent."
The very next day, a teacher invited her students to take part in a mock parliament event. "Each of you will represent a group," she explained carefully. "Every group must argue for or against ratifying a brand-new trade law." "What does ratification actually mean?" asked Zara, looking puzzled. "It means official approval," said the teacher warmly. "It is the step that makes a rule truly real."
Kian's team was chosen to represent the Union of Local Traders. Another group became the Coastline Confederation, while a third group played the part of the colonial ministers. Before the debate began, Kian spoke to his good friend Aran. "I need you to help me write a speech," he said. "We have to reflect the real lives of our people." "What do you want me to say?" Aran asked. "Tell them," Kian replied firmly, "that we will not accept more laws written without our consent. This is no longer just about trade, but about who we are." The day of the event arrived, and the school hall had been rearranged to look like a real government room.

Desks had been arranged in a wide circle, and at the front sat the students chosen to act as jurors, who would decide which argument was strongest. Kian stepped into the hall, his heart pounding hard. He looked around and saw his teacher nodding. "Speak your truth," she whispered.
The first group argued firmly in favour of the law. "It will increase our provisions," said their leader. "It will also bring harmony between the rulers and the local people." "But that harmony is forced," Kian answered, when at last it was his turn. "It's not harmony if we are not heard." He lifted a cloth-wrapped item and slowly unrolled it on the desk. "This is an instrument my father uses to measure wood. He taught me that you cannot build what you do not first understand. And yet these officials build laws without ever understanding us."
One of the jurors leaned forward. "What would you do instead?" "I would gather our community elders, market traders, boatmakers, and farmers," Kian said steadily. "I would ask them to reflect on what trade truly means to their families." "Has this ever been done before?" someone asked. "No," Kian admitted. "But it should have been. And it must happen now."
After the event, the teacher clapped warmly. "You have argued with determination and clarity." Later that day, Kian overheard a visiting student say, "That speech changed my perspective. I had never once thought of the law from the bottom." Another student added quietly, "It is a disgrace how long ordinary people were kept out of these decisions."
That night, at home, Kian told his father everything that had happened. "I have spoken," he said. "I told them that a real relationship must always travel in two directions." His father smiled with pride. "You have become a citizen today, Kian, not merely a student."
A week later, the real parliament finally arrived in Kalimani. They held a formal forum inside the council chamber, and Kian and Zara stood at the back with dozens of anxious villagers. One foreign official rose and spoke. "We will now vote to approve the new tariffs." A woman in the crowd stood up at once. "We object!" she shouted. Another voice added, "This is a disgrace! You cannot decide everything entirely alone!" Kian stepped forward bravely. "We demand entry into these talks. If you block our voices, you are building warfare without any guns." One minister frowned. "Children cannot speak in serious legal matters." "But who will live with the consequences?" Zara replied. "We will." Suddenly something shifted. A respected elder rose slowly from his seat. "I have spoken about justice for many years," he said, "but today I will finally practise it. Let them speak, and let them be heard."

In the days that followed, something quite unusual began to happen in Kalimani. The officials agreed to hold three full days of open hearings. One by one, the people entered the chamber and gave their honest testimonies. Fishermen spoke about the waters that had been blocked. Farmers described the unfair taxes they had paid for years. Traders listed the supplies and provisions that had never once been delivered.
One old man held up a battered copper pot. "This was made by a local inventor," he said. "He received no credit, no pay, and no name written anywhere. What would you call that, if it is not simple theft?" Each new voice added a little more pressure, and slowly something inside the old system began to shift. "Have you ever seen anything like this before?" Zara asked her mother that night. "Never," she replied softly. "But I have dreamed of it for a very long time."
Two weeks later, a large parchment was posted outside the market. "By shared vote, the parliament has ratified a revised trade law. Local leaders will now sit on the trade council. The blockades will end, and the tax rules will change. This law reflects your voice." That night, a joyful celebration filled the entire port. Drums echoed across the water, and fishermen danced with lengths of bright cloth waving in the air.
Kian stood quietly beside the tea stall, unsure of exactly what he felt. "I never truly imagined they would listen," he told Zara. "Maybe they never wanted to," she replied thoughtfully. "But in the end they had to. We simply made it impossible for them not to." A visiting scholar came to interview Kian. "Tell me," she said, "what do you think really changed the final outcome?" "It was not one single voice," he answered. "It was many voices, rising together. Not anger alone, but perspective and truth." The scholar smiled and said she would write about this remarkable day. "And I will keep on speaking," Kian said, "because there is still so much more to change. This is only the very first step."
The moral of this story is clear. Freedom begins not with noise, but with knowledge, courage, and many voices joined together in a shared purpose.

stories.title: When the Leaves Stop Speaking
stories.setting: A future East African research village beside a protected forest

parts.passageScript:
In the year 2083, in the green hills of what had once been northern Uganda, stood a protected grove named Nguvu Wa Asili, which means 'Power of Nature'. Around it lay a self-sustaining, multicultural research village where scientists, farmers, historians and community elders lived and worked together.
Amal, aged twelve, lived in the village. Her parents were both researchers at the local environmental agency, studying soil restoration and the water cycle. Amal loved science, but she also loved listening to the old stories her grandfather told.
'Did you know,' her grandfather would say, 'that long ago a traveller stood under that giant fig tree and promised that light would return after the world's sky broke?'
Amal grinned. 'You mean the supernova of 2081?'
'To me it was a promise; to you it is physics,' he smiled. 'But do not laugh. Some truths are shared in more than one language.'
That year the village was visited by a small agency of international scientists studying transpiration in old forests. 'The plants here release water at incredible rates,' said Doctor Alina, a biologist. 'It may be why the surrounding farmland stays so fertile.'
The villagers had always cared for the grove. Children were taught not to break branches, farmers planted food only at the edges, and elders and herbalists held monthly gatherings at the fig tree to thank the land for its rain. It was a place of peace.
But something was wrong. The outer ring of trees had begun to dry out.
'If the forest continues to deteriorate, the whole ecosystem will collapse,' warned Doctor Alina.
'What is causing it?' asked Amal.
'We are not sure yet,' she said. 'It may involve radiation leaking from a forgotten machine buried during the old wars. Or it could be a bacterial plague.'
Amal had questions. She asked her parents, she asked the scientists, and she even asked her grandfather. He stroked his beard. 'If the ground grows weak, perhaps it is because we stopped listening to it.'
'That is not science,' Amal said gently.
'It is a way of seeing,' he replied. 'And both ways matter.'
The scientists began testing the soil. Amal watched them gather tools and check the leaves for bacteria and radioactive particles. One sample glowed faintly blue. 'It is not dangerous in small amounts,' said Doctor Alina, 'but we should take it seriously.'

In the village square, meetings were held. A few leaders believed the outsiders were spreading propaganda, spreading fear so that they could seize control of the forest.
'This grove was originally ours to protect,' said one elder. 'Now it is filled with machines and measuring sticks!'
'It must be protected,' argued Amal's mother. 'If we lose it, we lose more than trees. We lose rainfall, clean air, even the ozone above us.'
'If pollution increases,' another scientist added, 'the ozone will keep breaking down.'
Amal began writing her own report. 'The forest,' she wrote, 'is both memory and machine. We must protect it. If we do nothing, its silence will grow loud.'
She collected data. She learned that transpiration had slowed in a quarter of the trees. Some leaves had changed texture, becoming dry and rough. Bark had peeled into strange shapes, like sculpture from a forgotten gallery.
'The change is not only chemical,' she told her mother. 'It feels personal.'
Her mother nodded. 'Sometimes places are like people. When they suffer, they give signs.'
'I want to make people care,' Amal later told Doctor Alina.
'Then make them see,' she replied. 'Use your imagination. Describe what will happen if this forest dies.'
Amal drew posters. One showed a mollusc dying beside a cracked streambed. Another showed the Earth wrapped in smog, a shrinking ecosystem floating like a translucent bubble in space. She built a display titled, 'If the leaves stop speaking, who will listen?'
At the youth assembly the following week, Amal gave a presentation. 'This forest is not just science,' she began. 'It is not just an old story. It is a library, a home and a memory.' She showed graphs, read her predictions and described the forest's architecture: its layers, patterns and hidden connections. 'You must not ignore the evidence. If we act now, we can save it.'
One student asked, 'What if the cause is unknown?'
'Then we keep learning,' Amal said. 'And we act where we can.'
A local carpenter had helped her build a model of the forest's root system, painted with hopeful words in several languages. 'Multicultural does not just mean people,' she explained. 'It means ideas, different ways of seeing, like science and tradition working together.'
The mayor was moved. 'Children,' he said, 'have reminded us of what we forgot. This forest is not ours to own; it is ours to tend.' The council agreed to ban further clearing near the grove. New funding went to clean-up crews and to careful radiation containment, and the agency announced a training programme for local youth.

That evening, Amal stood at the base of the fig tree again. The wind stirred the top branches gently.
Doctor Alina found her there. 'You have done more than observe,' she said. 'You have inspired people.'
Amal smiled. 'I only followed the data.'
'No,' her grandfather said, stepping out of the shadows. 'You followed your vision.'
Amal looked up at the tree that had watched over so many lifetimes. She thought about the restoration work that would begin in the morning, and about the renewable hope her display had promised.
'Some call it an old story,' she whispered. 'Some call it biology. Either way, it begins with belief, and with the choice to act.'
And the forest rustled softly in return, as if, at last, it had been heard.

stories.title: The Red Cloth
stories.setting: East African and familiar learner contexts

parts.passageScript:
The sun rose slowly over the hills of Kalembo, a village surrounded by dust and silence. Three months ago, everything had changed.
Foreign soldiers had arrived. They wore sharp grey coats and marched in tight rows. Without warning, they had proclaimed that Kalembo now belonged to a land “across the sea.” No one had seen this ruler. People called him a dictator, someone who gave orders no one could question.
The soldiers took control of the grain stores. They set up new laws in an administration centre — a stone building filled with papers and stamps. “This is what they call bureaucracy,” said the village elder. “A system where rules matter more than people.”
Twelve-year-old Amal had lived in Kalembo her whole life. She remembered laughter, music, and baskets of mangoes under the fig tree. Now she heard orders barked in a language she did not understand. People whispered more than they spoke, and soldiers watched every corner.
One day, a funeral was held for an old farmer who had refused to hand over his harvest. He had died quietly in his sleep, some said from starvation. A crowd gathered beside the river to mourn and bury him. Women wore shawls, men stood in silence, and children held hands.
Suddenly, a group of soldiers arrived. “No gatherings allowed!” one of them shouted. “This is a prohibited event.”
“But it is a funeral,” someone said.
“All events must be approved,” said the soldier. “Even grief must follow rules.”
The villagers dispersed slowly, heads bowed. But something stayed — an emotion deeper than sorrow. Frustration. Amal stood beside her mother and whispered, “They fear even our tears.”
That night, Amal asked her grandfather, “Why do they treat us this way?”
“Because people who oppress others are afraid,” he said. “They fear what they cannot control — memory, belief, unity.” She did not fully understand, but she remembered his words.
The next day, the soldiers painted warnings on walls: “Anyone who refuses to obey will be treated as treacherous.” The words were meant to scare, but they lit a fire in Amal’s heart. “These words,” she told her friend Leo, “are like weapons.”
“Then we need words too,” he said.
That night, they gathered red cloth scraps — bright, crimson, the colour the old farmer had worn when he walked through town. Amal’s mother had once called it “a colour no fear can hide.” Amal, Leo, and others tied the cloths on trees, water pots, and rooftops. On fences, they painted messages in charcoal: “This land has roots.” “We are people, not property.” They did not sign the messages, but the whole vicinity began to feel different. A wind of quiet courage blew through the village.

When the soldiers saw the red cloths, they grew angry. “Who is behind this?” they shouted. “These symbols are treacherous.” But no one spoke. It was a collective silence, and the villagers had found power in not revealing the truth.
The next day, all the cloths were torn down. But by sunset, new ones had appeared. At school, the teacher gave a new writing assignment: “Choose someone who showed courage. Write how they faced hardship, and how they responded.”
Amal wrote about her grandmother, who had once hidden refugees fleeing the war. “She was quiet,” Amal wrote, “but she acted. That is strength.” Leo wrote about a man named Kofi, an abolitionist who had fought slavery through song and secret messages.
Others wrote about leaders from the past. They used relative clauses naturally: “My grandmother, who raised me, believed in truth.” “Kofi, whose words became songs, never gave up.” “A soldier is someone who follows orders, which can destroy or protect.”
One morning, the soldiers arrived at school. “These books,” they said, “contain propaganda.” They burned several. “You must only learn what we allow.” Amal looked down, but something inside her refused to shrink.
That week, there were whispers of sickness. A health worker arrived from the capital to test the water. “This is a case of typhoid,” she said. “It is caused by unsafe drinking water.” She handed out carbon filters and gave instructions. “Boil your water. Avoid contaminated streams. Illness is not always observable. It hides.”
Later, Amal told Leo, “Injustice is like typhoid. You do not always see it, but it poisons everything.”
As the months passed, small changes grew. The soldiers patrolled less and shouted less. A new rule appeared: “You may bury your dead in groups of five or fewer.” “It is not freedom,” someone muttered, “but it is a crack in the wall.” Amal’s grandfather said, “It shows they feel pressure. They see we endure.”
The teacher asked the class to reflect: “What happens when people face power they cannot fight?” Amal raised her hand. “Some plant roots. Quiet ones. Ones that reach deep.” The crimson cloths returned, not just as symbols but in clothes, art, and flags.
One day, years later, a traveller came to Kalembo. He had heard of the red cloths, and he asked the villagers, “Who started the movement?” Amal, now older, pointed to a grave wrapped in crimson. “The man we buried,” she said. She pointed to a tree with painted bark. “The questions we asked.” Then she smiled. “And the girl I once was.”

stories.title: The Last Straits
stories.setting: East African and familiar learner contexts

parts.passageScript:
Long ago, before satellites mapped every coastline, explorers relied on wind, stars, and memory. In the heart of East Africa, a young physicist named Tariq joined a desert caravan setting out towards the unknown.
Their goal was to cross the Mzingi Straits, a mysterious water passage between two towering cliffs. No one had returned alive, but old maps claimed an extended river system ran beneath the cliffs. If it were true, the discovery could help small communities relocate and survive years of drought.
Tariq's team consisted of eight people: two experienced explorers, a weather expert in meteorology, a translator, and a group of local guides who knew the sands well. Each of them had made a serious commitment to the mission, not for glory, but to bring change.
The team's leader, Amara, stood before a map made of stitched cloth. Her hands, rough from years of expeditions, smoothed the fabric as if it held secrets.
'We will travel through harsh terrain,' she said. 'But if we succeed, this discovery will change how people understand the region.'
Tariq asked, 'What will we do if the riverbed is dry?'
'We will adapt,' Amara replied. 'The initiative depends on our resolve.'
Their first camp was near a cluster of acacia trees. Tariq set up a generator to power their tools. The machine hummed across the sand, pulsing like a second heart for the team.
'This generator is our lifeline,' he told the group. 'Without it, we cannot track the weather or charge our equipment.'
Each morning, they rose early to record data. Tariq explained the procedure to the younger guides.
'First, we collect samples. Then we label and store them carefully. Finally, we submit our findings to the agency.'
The young guides nodded. 'You are not like other outsiders,' one of them said. 'You explain things.'
Tariq smiled. 'Good science starts by listening.'
By the third week, the desert turned treacherous. Sandstorms appeared without warning. One storm destroyed their water cart.
'We must extend the trip,' Amara said. 'We will stop in the next territory for supplies.'
They relied on nearby nomads, who shared dried meat and sour milk in exchange for medicine and solar batteries.
'These people follow the herds and the stars,' Amara explained. 'They have navigated these sands for generations.'
At night, Tariq taught a young boy how to use the compass and read the clouds. In return, the boy sang desert songs that described the stars like friends.
One evening, just after dusk, a lone man arrived on camelback. His cloak was sun-bleached and torn, but his manner was sharp and calm.
'I am Karim,' he said. 'I have lived near the straits. I have seen what lies beyond.'
'An eyewitness account?' Amara asked. 'Can you describe it?'

'I saw water rushing like thunder,' Karim said. 'But I also saw markers, skulls set on posts. Someone refused to let strangers pass.'
'Who controls it now?' Tariq asked.
Karim shrugged. 'A forgotten civilisation, or a violent faction. Maybe both.'
Tariq looked again at the fading map. 'We will proceed carefully. We are not here to fight.'
The caravan reached the cliffs two days later. The wind screamed through the narrow passages. Rock carvings lined the stone, figures with long limbs and shields.
'This is a warning,' Karim said. 'But it is also confirmation.'
Using climbing gear, the team descended. At the base, they found smooth black stones, and in the cracks, cool mist was rising.
'There is water,' Tariq whispered. 'We were right.'
Then they saw dozens of footprints and a camp that had been abandoned recently. The fires were still warm. Tools lay half-buried in the dust.
'They must have relocated in a hurry,' Amara said. 'But why?'
Among the ashes, they found scraps of paper covered in code. One word had not burned: segregation.
Amara frowned. 'This is no longer just a river expedition. Someone tried to control who passed, and who drank.'
'Because if you control the land, you control the people,' Tariq said. 'And if you control the water, you control life.'
They set up a base higher on the ridge. Tariq reconnected the generator and began measuring the water speed, purity, and flow.
'We must regulate how this water is used,' he said. 'It cannot belong to any one group.'
Amara added, 'We are not just explorers. We are stewards of what we find.'
That night, the team wrote a proposal to explain what the land offered, and why it had to remain open.
'We propose an open science zone,' they wrote. 'This land should not be claimed by any one nation. Its production of clean water must support all the nearby communities. We must resist any system that repeats the segregation of the past.'
They added their predictions. If the area were claimed by force, violence would follow. If it were shared peacefully, migration and farming would improve.
'Real exploration begins with respect,' Tariq wrote. 'We do not own this place. We study, we learn, and we serve.'
As the team packed to leave, one member uncovered a rusted metal plate buried in the sand, its letters barely readable.
Karim pointed at it. 'A failed empire,' he said. 'They built walls, and they were erased.'
The journey home was long. Tariq taught the young guides to track the clouds and draw their own maps. In return, the boys sang to him, songs that had guided travellers for centuries.
Back in the capital, Amara delivered the report to the agency.
'The initiative is complete,' she said. 'But the river is still flowing.'
A year later, schools across East Africa studied the Mzingi discovery. Wells were dug. No flag flew over the cliffs, and the water remained free.

Years later, Tariq gave talks at universities about the expedition. 'What does science consist of?' he would ask. 'It consists of questions, care, and courage.'
He always ended with a photograph of Amara, Karim, the young guides, and himself, standing together by the straits with notebooks in hand and red cloths tied to signal peace.
'Explorers may map the land,' he would say. 'But true exploration maps the future.'
And deep beneath the cliffs, the river still ran, untouched and unowned, waiting for the next ones who would come, not to take, but to understand.

The first day at Mbali Academy was not what Amal expected.
She had been eagerly waiting to move into the school dormitory for weeks. Her mother said it would help her become more independent. Her father, who rarely shared his feelings, simply hugged her and said, "Remember who you are."
Amal was not sure what that meant. But she promised herself she would try.
Mbali Academy was a massive, stone-walled school perched on a green ridge. It was known for its fabulous science programme and its strict rules. Students wore uniforms and ate in long rows. The dormitories were clean but cold.
Her roommate was a girl named Nora, who talked firmly and fast.
"Don't touch my shelf," Nora said the moment Amal entered.
Amal smiled shyly. "I won't."
She unpacked her meagre belongings — two books, a tiny photo frame, and a borrowed jumper. Compared to Nora's colourful bedding and shiny decorations, Amal's side looked bare.
At dinner, Amal tried to talk to others. But most were already in their own friend groups. She felt a little uncomfortable, like a chair with one short leg.
"Just give it time," she told herself.
Later that week, a teacher announced that a new student council would be formed. "One student will be chosen from each dormitory group. They will help represent your voices and ideas."
Amal's ears perked up. Maybe this was her chance to be part of something.
The next morning, Amal saw a poster on the school notice board. "Nominate a student who shows leadership, kindness, and courage."
Nora and her friends giggled behind her.
"We already know who will win," Nora said. "Maya. Everyone likes her."
Amal looked at the names scribbled on the board. All were from the same friend group. None were new students. None were like her.
That night, she asked herself a question: should I try anyway?
"I don't belong," she whispered, frustrated.
But something inside her — small but substantial — told her to speak. She wrote her name in shaky handwriting.
The next day, whispers started. "Who is that girl?" someone asked.
"Amal," another replied. "Isn't she the one with the second-hand jumper?"
Nora rolled her eyes. "That's a questionable choice." Amal felt heat in her chest. She thought about removing her name. But a teacher passed by and said, "I saw your name. Good for you."
Amal smiled, just a little.
The council speeches were set for Friday. Students would gather in the hall. Each candidate had to give a short talk.
Amal felt as if her stomach had flipped. She barely slept on Thursday night.
"You don't have to do this," Nora said in the morning. "It's not too late to back out."
Amal looked at her reflection in the mirror. "I didn't come here to hide," she said quietly.

She remembered what her father had said.
When it was her turn to speak, Amal walked slowly to the front. Her paper trembled in her hands. She breathed in.
"My name is Amal. I'm new here, and I know I don't have a big group of friends yet. But I believe kindness should be a rule, not a suggestion."
She paused.
"Sometimes rules feel unavoidable, but that doesn't make them right. Some are even unconstitutional — they go against fairness."
The room was silent.
"I've felt frustrated and small here. But I've also learned that even small voices can grow. I will do my best to be fair, hospitable, and honest."
She stepped back. Her knees felt wobbly. The applause was quiet — but real.
Later, someone tapped her shoulder. A younger girl from another dormitory. "Thank you," the girl said. "I felt sensitive when I arrived too. You made me feel seen."
Amal smiled wide. It was not a massive moment, but it felt crucial.
Voting happened the next day. When the results were posted, Amal was not the winner. Maya had the most votes. But below her name, another line had been added: "Amal: assistant representative for dormitory two."
Amal nodded. "Maybe the rules adapted."
In the weeks that followed, she helped organise weekend activities, sorted out complaints, and reminded teachers when supplies were unavailable. She took the job seriously and learned quickly.
She noticed that when she spoke firmly, people listened. When she spoke aggressively, they pushed back. When she spoke dramatically, they laughed. She started choosing her tone more carefully.
One day, a rule was posted on the notice board: "Only students with full uniforms may attend weekend outings."
Several students could not afford new shoes. Amal raised her hand in the council meeting. "This rule," she said, "feels unfortunate and unfair. Some students try their best but do not have the means."
"It's about order," said a teacher.
"But order should never come before compassion," Amal replied.
Another representative whispered, "That rule sounds… unconstitutional."
They voted. The rule was changed. Amal felt her heart flutter. Change could be slow — but it was real.
One evening, she and Nora sat on their beds, both doing homework.
"You've changed," Nora said. "You used to be so quiet."
"I had to adapt," Amal replied. "And you?"
Nora shrugged. "I'm learning too. Being right all the time doesn't mean being respected."
They shared a laugh. It was small — but it felt honest.
During essay week, Amal wrote a piece called "Growing From the Middle." She used words like productive, symbiotic, and fragile.
"A school is like a tree," she wrote. "It needs deep roots of respect, branches of growth, and leaves that fall and come again. Every person here, whether popular or unpopular, makes it grow. Sometimes a fragile moment becomes the start of strength."
Her teacher wrote at the bottom, "Your voice is becoming more noticeable."
At the end of the term, Amal called home. "I didn't win," she told her father.
"But you changed something," he said. "That's better than winning."
She smiled. "I think I remembered who I was after all."

stories.title: Voices in the Courtroom
stories.setting: East African and familiar learner contexts

parts.passageScript:
The day of the trial felt different from every other in the town of Luyanda.
Shops opened more slowly. Motorbikes moved more quietly. Even the sky, usually so loud with birds, felt still.
Twelve-year-old Amal waited outside the school gate, clutching a folder full of papers. Her class was going on a field trip — not to the museum, or the zoo, but to the courtroom.
“We are currently observing a real case,” their teacher had said. “You’ll learn how rights, laws, and profession roles work in society.”
Amal had never stepped foot in a courthouse before. But she knew this was not a normal case.
It involved her neighbour, Mama Dina.
Mama Dina was a local food vendor who often gave Amal extra cassava or banana when she passed by. She was kind, wise, and popular. But last month, officials came to her stall and accused her of selling contaminated food.
They said her cooking water was unsafe. She was arrested, fined, and told she could no longer sell.
“I refuse to believe she did anything wrong,” Amal had told her parents.
“They say the test showed bacteria,” her mother had replied.
“She said the officer didn’t have her consent to test her pots,” Amal insisted.
“She told us,” her father added, “that the food wasn’t even served that day.”
Amal had listened to every word — and written it down. Now she carried those notes in her folder like evidence.
Inside the courthouse, rows of benches lined the walls. The room was full of murmurs. A judge in a black robe sat at the front. A commentator from the local radio station recorded notes for a short evening script.
The teacher handed out a sheet.
“Today, you will identify: the defence and prosecution; any compound nouns (such as tuition fees and legal penalties); verbs in present continuous; and new profession titles based on suffixes.”
Amal’s eyes danced across the list.
“The State v. Dina Okoro,” the bailiff announced.
A young physician testified first. “The test showed bacteria in the container,” he said. “Food from this water could cause illness.”
“But was food served that day?” asked the defence lawyer.
The physician hesitated. “We’re not currently sure.”
Amal scribbled: “Observation unclear. Present continuous used.”
Mama Dina’s commentary came next. She stood tall, her voice calm.
“The officer entered without asking. I never gave my consent. He touched my pots with gloves still dirty from the last stall. I told him: ‘That’s not allowed.’ But he wrote down his criticism anyway.”
Her lawyer nodded. “That’s reported speech. He said, she said.”

The teacher leaned over to Amal. “You’re doing good observation,” she whispered.
The prosecution argued that penalties must be applied equally. “All vendors must be inspected. Legal standards are there for a reason.”
“But,” Mama Dina’s lawyer said, “the process was flawed. If the action was unfair, the penalty is unconstitutional.”
Amal whispered to her classmate: “That means it goes against the rules of the country.”
The judge listened quietly, taking notes with a blue pen. His face revealed nothing.
After a break, the students gathered under a tree beside the courthouse.
“I still don’t understand,” one boy said. “If there were figures, like test results, doesn’t that mean she’s guilty?”
“But the figures might be wrong,” Amal argued. “And even good data needs good methods.”
“It’s like when you study heredity in science,” said a girl. “You can’t just assume something based on one test.”
Their teacher nodded. “Good thinking. Scientific wisdom applies in court too. Look at all sides.”
Back inside, a final witness spoke: a food safety commentator from the city.
“She is efficient, yes,” the woman said. “But during food checks, many women vendors are targeted more. We need more fair integration, not more bias or segregation.”
“Please avoid political speech,” said the prosecution.
But the judge replied, “Injustice is always political. Proceed.”
The trial ended, and the judge said he would return a verdict the next day.
As the students filed out, the teacher asked them to write a reflection.
“Today we saw how laws are made and used. But rules must be fair. When someone like Mama Dina is punished unfairly, people lose trust. Good observation is like science. It takes patience and care. I want to be a commentator, a legal advisor, or maybe a historian one day — someone who helps stories stay true.”
That night, Amal told her parents everything.
“She said the officer never washed his gloves. She said she never served that day.”
“She said the criticism was false,” her father added.
Her mother nodded. “She said the penalty wasn’t fair.”
“Exactly!” Amal smiled. “We all used reported speech. We all noticed the same things.”
The next morning, the town was waiting.
The judge read aloud: “The evidence was incomplete. The officer’s observation lacked protocol. The penalty is dropped. Mama Dina is free to return to her profession.”
Amal did not jump or cheer. She just grinned, wide and quiet.
The woman touched her shoulder. “Thank you. Your presence mattered.”
Amal felt her heart fill. It was a small moment — but powerful.
The next week, the students wrote scripts of the event for a class radio play. Amal helped add captions under printed photos, and even wrote the commentary for the narrator.

stories.title: The Speech Under the Baobab
stories.setting: Coastal and village communities facing natural events

parts.passageScript:
It was the dry season in Mbuma, and the dust hung low over the hills like a memory refusing to settle. A small congregation of villagers gathered beneath the baobab tree in the central square. Children whispered. Elders shifted their weight. Something important was coming.
Twelve-year-old Amal stood beside her grandfather, holding a folded sheet of paper in her hand. The administration had announced that students could now attend the weekly community forum, and Amal's school had chosen her to represent them.
"You will speak on behalf of the youth," Teacher Yasmin said. "It is called representation."
Amal's hands trembled, because her voice had never been heard by more than a classroom. Her grandfather placed a calm hand on her shoulder. "Speak the truth. Speak clearly. The baobab remembers."
Just days earlier, a big event had taken place in Mbuma. The local leader had made a public declaration that the economy would change. The country was leaving a capitalist model and adopting socialism, a system that promised fair distribution of wealth and public resources.
"We must shift towards equality," the leader had said. "Let us restore balance after years of unfair trade."
Many villagers had clapped, but others were worried. "What does socialism really mean?" someone had asked. "Will the shops close?" another whispered. "Could it cause inflation?" muttered Omar, a merchant. "My prices will have to rise."
Even Amal's parents were unsure. "Before, we had capitalism, with competition, ownership and private markets," her mother said. "Now they say we must share everything. It sounds better, but it worries me." "Systems are not just words," her father added. "They need care, not only promises."
The school had held a lesson on different systems. "Our current situation," said Teacher Yasmin, "comes from a capitalist model. But others include communism, where all resources are owned equally, and socialism, where things are shared fairly by law."
One boy raised his hand. "Which is better?" "That depends," the teacher replied. "Each system has its values and its failures." She drew three illustrations on the board: a market with coins, a factory with one large owner, and a shared field with many hands.
"Your task," she said, "is to write about which system could best help our village." Amal's group chose to write about restoration, about rebuilding after long hardship. They added a caption that said, "Shared power grows deep roots."
On forum day, Amal arrived early. Her classmate Sami joined her, carrying a chart with calculations that showed how food could be shared more fairly. "We used real data," he said. "With better distribution, we could feed forty more families every week."
Amal nodded. "But ideas must be spoken. Let us make sure we are heard."

The forum began with the head of the administration, who wore a beige suit and dark sunglasses.
"Citizens," he began, "we have started an initiative for change. This includes new trade agreements, updated copyright protections for local artists, and the expansion of modern farming machines, also known as mechanisation."
Amal listened carefully and scribbled notes: copyright means protecting ideas; mechanisation means machines that help farms. "But who benefits?" whispered Sami. "He did not say."
Then came the floor for community voices. An elder stood up. "I have farmed for forty years, and I do not understand these changes. Last week I tried to sell cassava and was told I needed a permit. My son says it is part of the new conversion system. What is that?"
The official responded, "We are converting from open selling to registered trade. It ensures fairer taxes." "But we are losing our freedom," the elder said, and the official looked away.
Next, a young woman spoke. "The new school fees are too high. I had to leave my studies because I could not afford them." A soft murmur spread through the crowd.
Then Omar the merchant spoke, sharp and direct. "The new system has potential, yes, but it also creates confusion. We used to know the rules. Now we are guessing." "It is a time of preparation," replied the official. "Change takes effort."
Finally, the moderator turned to the student speaker. "We welcome Amal." She stepped forward and felt the weight of every eye in the square.
"My name is Amal. I come as part of a new generation, but I speak with an old voice." She opened her folded paper. "While some were talking, others were planting. While systems changed, people still needed to eat. While the declaration was made, some children missed school."
The crowd was quiet. "We have studied capitalism, socialism, and communism. Each system speaks of justice, but justice is not automatic. It must be lived." She looked at the official. "You say there will be restoration. But we also ask: who decides what is restored? Who speaks for the ones without a microphone?"
Sami held up the chart. "With better calculation and careful distribution, no one needs to go hungry. The students have created models, and we ask that you review them."
There was a pause. Then a boy in the front row called out, "Go, Amal!" A few claps followed, then more. The official adjusted his tie. "We are revising our plans," he said slowly. "Perhaps we could meet the students next week."
After the forum, Amal sat beneath the baobab tree. "You did well," her grandfather said. "I spoke with my true expression," she replied. "And the baobab remembers," he said, smiling.

Later that month, new proposals were posted on the school notice board. The initiative would now include a council of student and teacher representatives, a review of the calculation methods used for food sharing, a declaration of student voices in community meetings, and a pilot programme for pollinator gardens and local pollination studies.
Amal's class created illustrations and wrote captions for each proposal. Sami added a note: "Representation is more than attendance. It is presence." The administration even added a line of its own: "Thanks to the students' commitment, the system grows stronger."
That weekend, a guest visited their classroom, a researcher from the city. "I have read your work," she told them. "I am preparing a historical excavation of local economies, and you have made a real impact."
"We are only twelve," said Sami, blinking. "Age does not limit insight," she replied, "just as systems do not limit dreams."
Amal raised her hand. "Could we write our own script? Something like a declaration of values for the next generation." The researcher nodded. "With your permission, I will even help you share it."
That evening, Amal walked home under a wide sky. She thought about allies and preparation, about restoration and hope, and about how a single clear voice could help a whole community stand together.

stories.title: The Scroll of Umbara
stories.setting: East African and familiar learner contexts

parts.passageScript:
In the dusty highlands of Umbara, beyond the modern suburbs and into the foothills of the great ridge, an unusual archaeological site was uncovered. It began with a single shovel hitting stone, and ended with a full team arriving, their equipment buzzing with electrical hum.
Fourteen-year-old Sami stood behind the caution tape, wide-eyed. He was not supposed to be there. But his uncle, a hospitable and generous site guard, had whispered, "Only if you watch quietly and don't touch anything."
What they found would change the region's understanding of history.
The object was a scroll, sealed in a jar, hidden deep in what seemed to be a cemetery from an ancient dynasty. The symbols were strange — part unknown, part familiar. The experts argued.
"A lost monarchy, possibly pre-feudal," said one scholar.
"Maybe classical influence mixed with native customs," said another.
"But it's been partially damaged," added a third. "The outer layer was churned by centuries of soil."
The writing team prepared a translation. "Some parts have been proclaimed, others must be reconstructed," the linguist explained.
They never expected the scroll to tell a story — with power, belief, and consequence.
A few lines had survived in full:
"In the Year of Eternal Fire, the Scholar of Umbara led his students to the Valley of Memory. There, a rehearsal was performed daily beneath the Great Tree. But a rebellion led by the Confederacy sought to destroy them. The Scholar was later imprisoned. Let the light remain."
Back in town, the news spread quickly.
"The Scholar's story could be proof of racial and cultural conflict long before colonial rule," one historian said.
"A new legacy rises from the soil," wrote a reporter from Paris, where international universities tracked African finds closely.
Others warned of being too excited.
"Don't build utopias from old bones," warned an elder. "We must understand, not dream."
Sami asked his history teacher, Teacher Yasmin, "Was the Scholar real?"
"We don't know," she said. "But history is often built from characteristics found in ruins, not full stories. That's why archaeological work is so valuable."
"But he was imprisoned," Sami whispered. "Why would someone do that to a scholar?"
She looked at him kindly. "Sometimes, new ideas scare people. Especially if it threatens a system — like a feudal or royal one."
Weeks passed. A local exhibit was prepared.
"Show the dynasty timeline," the curator instructed. "Add captions to each symbol."
An artist painted the admiral of the old guard, towering over a scene of chaos. In the corner, the Scholar stood calmly, eyes closed.
One placard read: "The Scholar's teachings were never fully recorded. But his students preserved fragments of his customs."

Another stated: "The movement was not just cultural — it was political. The Confederacy opposed his influence."
Sami stared at the map. One word whispered in his mind: terror.
He began writing in secret — building his own timeline of the Scholar's last days.
Using adverbs like "usually" and "often", he described the ceremonies performed at dusk.
Using the past passive, he wrote: "The scroll was hidden during the Confederacy's march. The Scholar was arrested. He was proclaimed a traitor. He was imprisoned."
He felt angry. But also fascinated.
Sami shared his writing with his grandmother.
"This is strong," she said. "But be careful. Tell the story — but don't become partial."
"Don't favour one side just because they seem gentle. Even peaceful leaders can make mistakes. That's what legacy means — it includes light and shadow."
The next week, Sami and his classmates visited the site officially.
They were told: "You may not touch artefacts. Do not step inside the cemetery. Observe only."
A researcher gave instructions: "Write a public report. Use imperatives and historical tone."
Sami's group wrote: "Document the Scholar's characteristics. List the systems — monarchy, Confederacy, feudal rule. Compare cultural and political causes of conflict. Include symbols from both classical and local tradition."
One student added, "Never forget what was done under orders."
Another added, "Include electrical sketches of the burial jars."
Sami drew a map with branching arrows: belief → rehearsal → fear → terror → legacy.
"Was imprisonment ever justified?" the teacher asked.
"No!" one girl said. "It's cruel."
"But if the Scholar was threatening the monarchy, they saw it as control," another said.
"But belief isn't a weapon," Sami replied. "He was trying to help."
"Maybe," said another. "But we weren't there."
They were told to write essays using evidence.
Sami's title: "Imprisoned Memory: Systems That Fear New Ideas."
In the final week, Sami stood at the exhibit as a student guide. Tourists asked him questions.
"What makes this story special?" one woman asked.
Sami answered, "Because we don't know everything. That makes it ours to explore."
He used clear verbs: proclaimed, imprisoned, discovered.
He pointed to the scroll. "That was partially burned — but its message lived."
One visitor from Merrimack, a teacher, told Sami, "In our schools, we don't teach about African scholars."
"You should," Sami said. "The Scholar was buried. But not forgotten."
On the last day, a candlelight tribute was held. It wasn't a ceremony. Just respectful.
"This land remembers. The scroll returned. We are not students of history. We are its writers."
And under the fading baobab tree, Sami whispered, "The Scholar was buried, but not forgotten — and now his story has a writer."

stories.title: The Children of Wind Valley
stories.setting: East African and familiar learner contexts

parts.passageScript:
The village of Lusinga rested in a wide valley surrounded by high ridges and evergreen trees. It was once famous for its cool climate, its wildflowers, and the strong winds that whispered through the hills. But recently, the land had begun to suffer.
"There used to be so many trees here," said Amara, age 13, as she climbed a slope with her twin brother, Kofi. "Now look at this mess."
The mountain landscape was dry. Broken stumps replaced the old forest trails. Empty cans and torn plastic hung on the fallen branches. People had cleared much of the forest for firewood and farming. It was called deforestation, and it had changed everything.
"Even the wind feels wrong," said Kofi. "It is hotter now. The streams have dried up. And the peppermint plants are gone."
They sat on a rock overlooking the valley.
"We need to do something," Amara said.
At school the next day, their science teacher announced a project. "You will design a plan to help the environment," she said. "This region has suffered. Now it is your turn to help it recover."
"What can we do?" asked a boy.
"That is for you to analyse," she replied. "It may involve new tools, new rules, or even a new way of thinking."
The students were excited. Amara and Kofi formed a group with their classmates Imani and Tariq. They named their group The Children of Wind Valley.
The first thing they did was research. "We have already lost sixty per cent of our forest," said Imani, reading aloud. "Many animals have relocated. The soil is dry. And we have had more floods this year than ever before."
Kofi pointed at a graph. "Temperatures have climbed, too. This valley used to be cooler. Now it is close to the subtropics."
Tariq nodded. "My grandmother says the wind used to sing. Now it screams."
They decided on a goal: to preserve what was left and replant what had been lost. They made posters and maps, and Tariq wrote all their titles in neat cursive. One poster said: "Plant. Protect. Pass it on." Imani added a caption: "Wind Valley is our heritage. Nature is not just space; it is memory."
They visited a local farm with a wind turbine, and the farmer explained how it worked. "The turbine collects the wind's power and turns it into electricity," he said.
"Could we build a small one at school?" Kofi asked.
"With the right support," the farmer replied. "You would need planning, commitment, and money."
The team met under the big fig tree after school. Imani held up a drawing. "Imagine it," she said. "A small wind farm. A tree nursery. A learning centre."
"It will take real sacrifice," said Amara. "Time, energy, and patience. Maybe some people will not like it."

"But it could be a model for other schools," said Tariq. "A thriving space for nature and learning." They called it the Ridge Replanting Project.
They wrote a proposal using the present perfect: "We have measured changes in temperature and soil quality. We have mapped the affected zones. We have spoken to local farmers and elders."
They practised the future tense too: "We will plant one hundred trees. We will build a wind model. We will create a new environmental club."
They used clear adjective order as well, describing "a small wooden solar-powered nursery" and "a wide circular concrete platform."
Not everyone supported them. "This is just school talk," said a shopkeeper. "It is not real." One man shouted, "Stop blaming us for cutting trees! Do you want us to starve?" Some accused the group of trying to overthrow tradition.
"That is not our goal," Amara said in a public meeting. "We are not blaming. We are planting. Not to destroy the past, but to protect the future."
The district officer, Ms. Alina, came to their school. "I have read your proposal," she said. "It is detailed and powerful, especially your section on reform." She showed them her notes. "You have used real data, honest writing, and a clear vision."
"Will we get support?" Amara asked.
"You have earned a pilot grant," she said. "It is enough for fifty seedlings and a model turbine. But you must monitor everything and report each week."
They were amazed. "We did it!" said Imani.
That weekend, they began planting. Students dug holes and elders helped carry compost. A local artist painted a sign: "This ridge is a pluralistic place, where animals, trees, and children all belong."
They cleaned an old storehouse and turned it into a learning room, which they called The Green Room. Inside, Amara taped a sign on the wall: "We have sacrificed comfort for hope. We have collided with doubt. But this is our space of transformation."
By the end of the term, forty-seven trees had survived. Bees returned. Butterflies fluttered near the new flowers. Some peppermint bushes sprouted again.
The school held an open day. Visitors toured the ridge and the Green Room, and many said it was beautiful. Occasionally, someone still called it "just a school project."
Then a letter arrived, from a school in Rwanda: "We heard about your work. Could you send us your report? We want to start something too."
In the final assembly, the principal read from their first submission: "We believe in caring for the environment through education and respect. The wind has shaped our stories. Now we shape the wind."
Outside, the wind turned again, this time softer. The trees moved gently, and the ridge whispered. Amara smiled. "They said we could not change anything," she said. "And yet," said Kofi, "we have changed everything."
